title: Flaw
summary: The most common LR question. Find the gap, name it in general terms, then check each choice: did the author do this, and is it a problem?

slides.title: Describe the mistake
body: A flaw question asks you to describe what is wrong with the argument. You don’t fix it or attack it; you name it.

The right answer is a general description of the error, often in abstract language: “takes for granted that…”, “fails to consider…”, “confuses…”. Your prediction should be in plain words; then you translate.
slides.callout: Two checks for every choice: did the author actually do this, and is it actually a problem here?

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument…
The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it…
Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the argument?
The argument's reasoning is questionable in that the argument…
slides.note: “Vulnerable to criticism” and “questionable” mean the same as “flawed”.

steps.label: Conclusion and evidence
steps.do: Find the main conclusion and the premises offered for it. Ignore background and opposing views.

steps.label: Name the gap
steps.do: Assuming the premises are true, why doesn’t the conclusion follow? Say it in a few words: bad sample, cause from correlation, ignores another explanation.

steps.label: Translate
steps.do: Turn your plain-words flaw into the test’s language. A sample problem becomes “relies on a group that may not be representative”.

steps.label: Two checks
steps.do: For each choice: did the author do this? If yes, is it a real problem for this argument? A choice must pass both.

steps.label: Break long choices
steps.do: Split a wordy choice into parts and test each part against the argument. One false part sinks the choice.

slides.title: Level 1: the method, step by step
slides.stimulus: Pollster: In a survey of readers of Outdoor Living magazine, 82 percent said they support expanding the state park system. Clearly, most voters in the state would support a ballot measure to expand the park system.
slides.stem: The reasoning in the pollster's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: fails to consider that readers may support expanding the park system for different reasons
choices.B: treats the opinion of an expert as if it settled the question
choices.C: relies on a group whose views may differ systematically from those of voters in general
choices.D: confuses the percentage of readers who support expansion with the number of readers
choices.E: assumes that what is true of most voters must be true of each voter

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.note: Most voters in the state would support expanding the park system.
steps.highlight: most voters in the state would support a ballot measure to expand the park system

steps.label: Evidence
steps.note: 82 percent of one magazine’s readers support it.
steps.highlight: In a survey of readers of Outdoor Living magazine

steps.label: Name the gap
steps.note: Readers of an outdoors magazine are not a typical cross-section of voters. Bad sample.

steps.label: Two checks
steps.note: Look for the choice that says the group may not represent voters. Make sure the author really did what each choice claims.

why.A: Did it happen? Yes, the pollster ignores reasons. Is it a problem? No: support is support, whatever the reason.
why.B: Didn't happen. No expert is cited.
why.C: Correct. Outdoor-magazine readers are likely to favor parks more than voters as a whole.
why.D: Didn't happen. The conclusion is about a majority of voters, not a number of readers.
why.E: Didn't happen. The argument says nothing about each individual voter.

slides.title: Level 2: a link mistaken for a cause
slides.stimulus: Teachers at Fairmont Middle School, which serves about nine hundred students, have noticed that students who eat the school's free breakfast earn higher grades, on average, than students who do not. The program is voluntary: each student decides whether to take part. The teachers conclude that the breakfast program improves students' grades, and they urge the district to fund it for another four years.
slides.stem: The teachers' reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: bases its conclusion on the teachers' general impressions rather than on grades that were actually measured and recorded
choices.B: overlooks that students who choose to eat breakfast at school may differ from the others in ways that affect grades
choices.C: fails to consider that the program may help some students a good deal more than it helps other students
choices.D: ignores the cost to the district of funding the breakfast program for another four years
choices.E: assumes that what holds for the average student at the school holds for every single student there

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.highlight: the breakfast program improves students' grades

steps.label: Evidence
steps.note: Breakfast eaters have higher average grades than non-eaters.
steps.highlight: students who eat the school's free breakfast earn higher grades, on average, than students who do not

steps.label: Name the gap
steps.note: A link between two things does not show one causes the other. Students who opt in may already be more motivated or have steadier mornings.
steps.highlight: The program is voluntary: each student decides whether to take part.

steps.label: Two checks
steps.note: C and D are true of the argument, but neither matters. The conclusion is about whether the program raises grades, not for whom or at what cost.

why.A: Didn't happen. The teachers cite grades, which are measured, not impressions.
why.B: Correct. Students who opt in may differ in motivation, which would explain the higher grades without any help from the breakfast.
why.C: Happened, harmless. Uneven benefit would not undercut the claim that the program improves grades.
why.D: Happened, harmless. The conclusion is about effect on grades, so cost is beside the point.
why.E: Didn't happen. The teachers speak of averages and make no claim about every single student.

slides.title: Level 3: one cause does not cancel another
slides.stimulus: Commentators have long blamed the decline of the Torrance River's trout population on warming water. Biologists confirm that the river has warmed by about two degrees over the period. A recent survey, however, found that the number of otters along the river has more than doubled over the same period, and otters feed heavily on trout. Since the otters' appetite alone can account for a substantial share of the losses, the commentators' explanation must be rejected: warming of the water cannot have contributed to the decline in any way.
slides.stem: The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: presumes, without offering any support, that the commentators' temperature measurements of the river were inaccurate
choices.B: draws a conclusion about every fish species in the river from evidence about trout alone
choices.C: fails to show that the otters account for a larger share of the decline in trout than the warming water does
choices.D: overlooks the possibility that the otters' numbers rose for reasons that are entirely unrelated to the water temperature
choices.E: takes the fact that one factor accounts for a substantial share of a decline to show that no other factor contributed to it

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.note: Warming cannot have contributed at all.
steps.highlight: warming of the water cannot have contributed to the decline in any way

steps.label: Evidence
steps.note: Otters doubled, and their appetite can explain a substantial share of the losses.
steps.highlight: the otters' appetite alone can account for a substantial share of the losses

steps.label: Name the gap
steps.note: A substantial share is not the whole. Two factors can both add to a decline. The author treats them as rivals.

steps.label: Name the traps
steps.note: C is tempting but it is about which factor is bigger. Even a smaller share would refute 'in any way'. D asks why otters rose, which does not touch whether warming also added to the losses.

steps.label: Confirm
steps.note: E names the leap: one factor explains part, so no other factor can have played a part.

why.A: Didn't happen. The argument accepts that the water warmed and never questions the measurements.
why.B: Didn't happen. The conclusion is about trout only.
why.C: Tempting, but wrong target. Even if otters explained more, warming could still have contributed, so the comparison does not repair the gap.
why.D: Happened, harmless. Why the otters increased has no bearing on whether warming also contributed.
why.E: Correct. Explaining part of the decline with otters does not rule out a second factor, yet the argument says warming 'cannot have contributed in any way'.

slides.title: Level 4: sufficient pair run backward
slides.stimulus: The park's posted rules say that anyone who both completes the full trail and holds a valid permit is allowed to camp at Ridge Lake. A ranger confirmed on Saturday, during a routine check of the lakeside campsites, that Priya, a regular visitor, is allowed to camp there and that she holds a valid permit. Because the permit is one of the two things the rules require, and Priya has it, the only open question is whether she completed the full trail. Since she is allowed to camp at the lake, she must have.
slides.stem: The reasoning in the argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.A: treats a pair of conditions that together suffice for an outcome as though one of those conditions were required for it
choices.B: treats a condition that is required for an outcome as though that condition alone were enough to bring the outcome about
choices.C: infers that a person lacks one qualification from the fact that the person has the other qualification
choices.D: draws a conclusion about every visitor to the park from the case of one visitor who was found at the lake
choices.E: uses the word 'allowed' in one sense in its premises and in a different sense in its conclusion

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.highlight: the only open question is whether she completed the full trail

steps.label: Evidence
steps.note: She is allowed to camp, and she has a valid permit.
steps.highlight: is allowed to camp there and that she holds a valid permit

steps.label: Read the rule
steps.note: Trail plus permit is enough to be allowed. The rule never says it is the only way, and it never says each part is required.
steps.highlight: anyone who both completes the full trail and holds a valid permit is allowed to camp at Ridge Lake

steps.label: Name the gap
steps.note: The argument runs the rule backward: allowed, so the trail was done. Another route to being allowed could exist.

steps.label: Kill the near twin
steps.note: B names the opposite error. The word to check is 'required'. The rule gives a sufficient pair, and the argument treats part of it as required. B describes required treated as enough.

why.A: Correct. The pair 'trail plus permit' is enough for being allowed. The argument treats the trail as something being allowed requires.
why.B: The reverse error. Here a sufficient pair is treated as required. B describes a required condition treated as enough, so it does not fit.
why.C: Didn't happen. The argument never concludes that Priya lacks a qualification.
why.D: Didn't happen. The conclusion is about Priya alone.
why.E: Didn't happen. 'Allowed' means the same thing in the premises and in the conclusion.

traps.name: Didn’t happen
traps.tell: Describes a real flaw that this argument doesn’t commit. Check it against the text.

traps.name: Happened, harmless
traps.tell: The author did this, but it doesn’t hurt the argument, like ignoring people’s motives when only their votes matter.

traps.name: Wrong flaw family
traps.tell: The reverse of the actual error: “assumes it is sufficient” when the argument treated it as necessary.

traps.name: Real-world complaint
traps.tell: Objects that a premise is false or a conclusion is unfair. Premises are accepted as true; only the reasoning is on trial.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Name the flaw in plain words before the choices.
Translate to test language: takes for granted, fails to consider, confuses.
Every choice: did it happen, and does it matter?
Premises are true; only the leap is wrong.
